title: Ripples become an ocean
hookLine: one glimpse swallows Ajamila's life; the sutras on ripples and who crosses
carry: dussanga turns ripples into an ocean
tomorrow: A taste that can't be told

cards: In the Bhagavata Purana, Ajamila is a young Brahmin with a good name: learned, gentle, careful in his duties. One day his father sends him to the forest for flowers and kindling.
On the way home he sees a man and a woman of the town, drunk and laughing in each other's arms. It's one glimpse. He tries to steady his mind with all he's studied, and can't.
He keeps thinking of her, keeps going back, and the thought is fed until it swallows everything: his father's wealth, his young wife, his good name.
Today the Narada Bhakti Sutras give that a picture: ripples becoming an ocean.

teach.b: Bad company, dussanga, is to be given up in every way, the sutras say. And they give the reason as a chain.
It causes desire, then anger, then delusion, then the loss of memory, then the loss of understanding, and then the loss of everything.
Then the image: though these arise only like ripples, through company they become an ocean. A flash of desire or anger isn't a disaster in itself. A ripple is a ripple.
What turns it into an ocean is company: whatever keeps feeding it, a person, a place, a feed on a screen. Many teachers read Ajamila's fall exactly this way: one glimpse, fed day after day.
Then a question, asked twice: who crosses? Who crosses over maya, the great illusion? The answers come in short lines.
The one who gives up clinging, serves the great, becomes free of mine, goes beyond the pairs of opposites, like pleasure and pain, and comes to a love that doesn't break off.
That one crosses, that one crosses, and helps the worlds cross too.
And Ajamila? You met his ending in earlier years: old and afraid of death, he called his son's name, Narayana, and Vishnu's messengers came.
The Bhagavata says he then went to Haridwar on the Ganga and gave his last years to devotion. Even the man the ocean swallowed got across.
That's why Hindu families guard their company and seek out satsang: in this teaching, the mind takes the shape of what it keeps near.

how: Devotional teachers explain the sutras on bad company as advice to guard the mind, and pair it with the positive practice of satsang, keeping company that nourishes love of God.

o: a crowd of friends who share your faith
love of God, kept from company that feeds ripples
a festival held each year on the shore of the sea

games.q: ripples and crossing — tap the pairs.
p: bad company, to be given up

s: the sutras say a single flash of anger is a disaster
they call these ripples. it's company that feeds them into an ocean.
the sutras ask 'who crosses?' twice and answer twice
who crosses, who crosses maya? that one crosses, that one crosses.
in the sutras, the one who crosses simply leaves the world behind
the last phrase is: and helps the worlds cross too.

games.q: a small irritation rises in you. the sutras call it a ripple. what turns it into an ocean?
o: the company that keeps feeding it.
games.why: though these arise like ripples, the sutras say, through company they become an ocean.

practice: Sooner or later something will rise, an irritation, a wanting, a worry; notice it the way you'd notice a ripple on water.
Don't push it down and don't feed it, no replaying the argument, no adding the next thought; just watch it rise and flatten out on its own. If you pray, you can hand each ripple to God as it passes.

wordCard.voice: Bhakti. In the sutras, it's guarded from the company that turns ripples into an ocean, and it carries those who cross.

orig.note: Sanskrit duḥsaṅga, bad company: the sutras say it is to be given up in every way.

carryVoice: Your line: dussanga turns ripples into an ocean. A ripple left unfed stays a ripple. Rest well.

sources.ref: Narada Bhakti Sutras 43–50 (bad company; the chain of losses; ripples become an ocean; who crosses maya; he crosses and helps the worlds cross)
